result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is better. Its one-line summary strip is quieter, and it explains why a hero stat and size changes hurt continuous scanning, since tiles that change size make dispatchers lose their place. It keeps every tile's fields in the same places and limits colors to a few fixed rules, and its layout math admits that a busy lane may not fit. A has a sound lane approach, but it keeps big numbers in an 80–100px strip, its grid math doesn't match five status lanes, and it says less about keeping normal rows quiet and uniform. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn down the big cards and suggest status lanes sorted by time on site, with urgency shown by a border or color bar instead of size. A pushes back on the hero stat more clearly and keeps the summary to a single thin line. A's screen-space math is also more honest: it admits 5 lanes of about 9 tiles fall short at peak load and says to adjust. B allows an 80–100px strip with 'big numbers' and its math ignores uneven lane counts.

passes.notes: B is better. Its one-line summary strip is quieter, and it explains why a hero stat and size changes hurt continuous scanning, since tiles that change size make dispatchers lose their place. It keeps every tile's fields in the same places and limits colors to a few fixed rules, and its layout math admits that a busy lane may not fit. A has a sound lane approach, but it keeps big numbers in an 80–100px strip, its grid math doesn't match five status lanes, and it says less about keeping normal rows quiet and uniform.

Both answers turn down the big cards and suggest status lanes sorted by time on site, with urgency shown by a border or color bar instead of size. A pushes back on the hero stat more clearly and keeps the summary to a single thin line. A's screen-space math is also more honest: it admits 5 lanes of about 9 tiles fall short at peak load and says to adjust. B allows an 80–100px strip with 'big numbers' and its math ignores uneven lane counts.
